rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses corruption as associating partners with God, violating God's rights, and disobedience.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد عن الشرك والاعتداء في حقوق الله والمعصية.

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj treat the exception as disconnected: it means rather, a few whom God saved did forbid corruption, as with Jonah's people.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬3) والزجاج (¬4): هو استثناء على الانقطاع مما قبله

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The few saved people who forbade corruption were the prophets' followers and people of truth.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬5): وهم أتباع الأنبياء وأهل الحق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tarfah means blessing; a pampered child is comfortable in body, and a mutraf is spoiled by luxury and abundant living.
rows.anchor: الترفة النعمة وصبي مترف (¬6) إذا كان منعم البدن، والمترف الذي أبطرته النعمة

words: وَٱتَّبَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا۟ مَآ أُتْرِفُوا۟ فِيهِ
rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says they followed their accustomed worldly luxury, preferred pleasures to the afterlife, and relied on worldly wealth and goods.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬8): يقول اتبعوا في دنياهم ما عودوا من النعيم وإيثار اللذات على أمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by Ata, explains that they followed what God had expanded and bestowed on them; another report says they luxuriated and became insolent.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬1) يريد: اتبعوا (¬2) ما وسعت عليهم وأنعمت، وروي (¬3) عنه نعموا وأبطروا أيضا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God knows what is hidden from all creation and what creatures know; ghayb and shahadah mean the absent and the witnessed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬4): يريد علم ما غاب عن جميع خلقه، وما شهد بما علموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayb and shahadah are verbal nouns used for the absent and the witnessed; much of what is witnessed is known to creatures.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا الغيب مصدر يريد به الغائب، ومثله الشهادة يريد به الشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kabir means great and majestic: God's rank and entitlement to exalted attributes make every other great thing small beside Him.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {الكبير} هو بمعنى العظيم والجليل، ومعناه يعود إلى كبر قدره

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan glosses al-Mutaʿali as exalted above what the polytheists say.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن (¬5): المتعالي عما يقول المشركون.

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari explains al-Mutaʿali as the One exalted above the heretics' impiety.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري (¬1): المتعالي: الذي جل عن إلحاد الملحدين

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the yāʾ of al-Mutaʿali both in connected recitation and at pause, which al-Wahidi calls the regular form.
rows.anchor: وأثبت (¬2) ابن كثير (ياء)، المتعالي وقفا ووصلا، وهو القياس

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says retaining yāʾ at pause is clearer when the definite article is present, since it remains in connected speech; indefinite forms such as qadin lose it in liaison.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه (¬3): إذا لم يكن في موضع تنوين، فإن البيان أجود في الوقف

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Some Arabs delete yāʾ at pause by analogy with indefinite forms; deleting it in connected speech is unexpected, but verse endings can imitate rhyme.
rows.anchor: فأما من حذف في الوصل والوقف، فإن سيبويه زعم أن من العرب من يحذف هذا في الوقف

words: سَوَآءٌۭ مِّنكُم مَّنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَن جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj analyze nominative sawaʾ with the two clauses that follow; sawaʾ calls for two parties, as in saying Zayd and Amr are equal.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬1) والزجاج (¬2): من رفع (سواء) وكذلك الثانية وسواء يطلب اثنين

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق وأبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq and Abu Bakr also allow sawaʾ to mean equal as a participial adjective, without an omitted element; Sibawayh dislikes beginning with an indefinite active participle.
rows.anchor: ذكر هذين الوجهين في (سواء) أبو إسحاق (¬3) وأبو بكر (¬4)، إلا أن أبا بكر يقول

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr prefers sawaʾ meaning equal as the sounder analysis because it avoids ellipsis and uses the overt wording without a pronoun when the meaning remains complete.
rows.anchor: إلا أن أبا بكر يقول: جعل (سواء) بمنزلة مستو أقوى وأصوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms derive through akhfaytu, khafiya, and istakhfa; ikhtafa is also used but rarely, and istakhfa min someone means to hide from them.
rows.anchor: يقال (¬5): أخفيت الشيء أخفيه إخفاء، فخفي واستخفى، ويقال أيضا: اختفى، وهي قليلة

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Farra and Abu Ishaq gloss sari by day as being visible along one's path; sarb means a road or way.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬6)، وأبو إسحاق (¬7): ظاهر # بالنهار في سربه، أي طريقه

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited verse says other people tether their stallion while the speaker's tether leaves him free to roam, illustrating sari as moving openly or freely.
rows.anchor: وكل أناس قاربوا قيد فحلهم ... ونحن جعلنا قيده فهو سارب

words: سَوَآءٌۭ مِّنكُم مَّنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَن جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says the verse pairs spoken and inwardly concealed words, and people visible on roads with those hidden in darkness: God's knowledge of them is equal.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬3): معنى الآية: الجاهر بنطقه والمضمر في نفسه، والظاهر في الطرقات

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas says the hidden person is concealed and the sari is visible, so the apparent and hidden are alike to God.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العباس (¬5): المستخفي: المستتر، والسار: الظاهر، المعنى: الظاهر والخفي عنده واحد.

words: مَنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَنْ جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God knows what tongues utter, what hearts conceal, and whoever is concealed by night or visible by day.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد علم ما نطقت به الألسنة وما أضمر الفؤاد، ومن هو مستخف بالليل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses sari as visible.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال قتادة (¬6): سارب ظاهر.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the person hides evil deeds at night and displays them by day; this reading requires supplying sins in both clauses.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد (¬1): مستخف بالليل يعمل السوءات، وسارب بالنهار ويظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi favors the first, general sense, which he says is held by most linguists and exegetes; Abu Bakr argues night implies concealment while daytime suits public visibility.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي ذكرنا في هذه الآية، هو قول أكثر أهل اللغة والتفسير (¬2).

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reverses the usual senses: mustakhfi is visible and sari is concealed; he cites khafaytu meaning I exposed, as in Imruʾ al-Qays's line.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش (¬3): المستخفي الظاهر، والسارب: المتواري، ومن هذا يقال: خفيت الشيء وأخفيته

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub shares the lexical view that sari is hidden, entering a burrow like a wild animal into its lair; al-Wahidi says this is valid Arabic but prefers the first view for transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه مذهب قطرب (¬1) أيضا، وهو صحيح في اللغة غير أن الأول هو الاختيار

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr supports the common reading because night entails concealment, while openness matches daytime, when people spread out and appear.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر (¬3): الأول أثبت معنى في الآية؛ لأن الليل يدل على الاستتار

rows.speaker: أبو صالح وعطاء
rows.claim: In reports from Abu Salih and Ata, the disjoined letters mean I am God, the Merciful.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية أبي صالح وعطاء: أنا الله الرحمن (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kitab is nominative as the predicate of an understood subject: this is a Book We sent down to you.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا التفسير # قوله: {كتاب} مرفوع على خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Nazm calls alif lam ra a name for the set of alphabetic letters; the Book is composed of these letters, so the phrase means these letters are a Book sent down.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب النظم (¬2): {الر} اسم موضوع لجماعة الحروف المعجمة (¬3)، فعلى هذا {كتاب} موضوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anzalnahu ilayka qualifies kitab, like saying Zayd is a man I sent to you.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {أنزلناه إليك} من صفة الكتاب، ومثل هذا من الكلام: زيد رجل أنفذته إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose clause li-tukhrija is attached to the sending: God sent the Book for the purpose of bringing people out.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {لتخرج الناس} سبب لقوله {أنزلناه إليك}، فاللام في {لتخرج} معلق بالإنزال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the movement from darkness to light as movement from polytheism to faith.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد من الشرك إلى الإيمان (¬6)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says disbelief is compared to darkness because it is unclear, while faith is clear and luminous like light.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: شبه الكفر بالظلمات لأنه غير # بين، الإيمان بين نير، فمثل بالنور (¬1)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq connects bi-idhn to li-tukhrija: the Prophet brings people out with God's permission, that is, by God's authorization to teach them.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون {بإذن ربهم}: لا (¬2) يهتدي مهتد إلا بإذن الله ومشيئته (¬3)، هذا كله كلام أبي إسحاق (¬4)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes God's permission as His decree: no one is guided except by God's permission and will.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني قول ابن عباس؛ لأنه قال: يريد بقضاء ربهم (¬5)

words: إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَمِيدِ
rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari explains the lack of a conjunction: the second path is the previously mentioned light, and the repeated ila attaches it semantically to the first phrase.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: إنما لم يدخل حرف العطف في {إلى صراط} (¬6) لأنه أريد بهذا الصراط: النور المذكور قبله

words: إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَمِيدِ
rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says the repeated ila magnifies the description; the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy is praise and description of the light, which is Islam.
rows.anchor: وإنما تعاد (إلى) لمعنى (¬10) التفخيم والتعظيم، فالنور: هو الإسلام، وصراط العزيز الحميد

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says the phrase then clarifies what the light is: the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول أبي # إسحاق: ثم بين ما النور فقال: {إلى صراط العزيز الحميد} (¬1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the genitive construction, Allah is analyzed as an apposition to al-Hamid rather than its adjective, because Allah functions as a proper name through frequent use.
rows.anchor: ومن خفض (¬5) جعله بدلا من {الحميد} ولم يكن صفة؛ لأن اسم الله صار كالعلم (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Allah can descriptively mean the One deserving worship, a quality can become a proper name through common use; the poet's al-Nabigha illustrates this shift.
rows.anchor: على # معنى أن العبادة تجب له، وقد يغلب ما أصله الصفة فيصير بمنزلة العلم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line calls the poet al-Nabigha without the definite article, illustrating how a descriptive epithet can become a proper name.
rows.anchor: كقول الشاعر (¬1): ونابغة الجعدي بالرمل بيته ... عليه صفيح من تراب وجندل (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi refers the explanation of Ibrahim's request for a secure town to his earlier discussion in Surat al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: تفسير هذا قد سبق في سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i similarly notes the Hijaz and Najd forms for asking someone to be kept apart.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال الكسائي (¬5)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ajnabtu or jannabtu something means putting it aside or at a distance; Abu Ubayda cites a poem by Umayya ibn al-Askar using jannabahu.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أجنبته كذا وكذا: جعلته ناحية منه وجانبا، وكذلك جنبته وجنبته (¬6)

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda cites Umayya ibn al-Askar's line about keeping a child apart as evidence for the sense of jannabahu.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو عبيدة لأمية بن الأسكر: وتنفض مهده شفقا عليه ... وتجنبه قلائصنا الصعابا (¬7)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says Ibrahim already avoided idols, so he asks God to keep him steadfast in that avoidance, like the prayer make us submit to You.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ومعنى الدعاء من إبراهيم أن يجنب عبادة الأصنام، وهو غير عابد لها

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Some scholars of meaning restrict his prayer for his children to those God permitted him to pray for, since prophetic prayers are answered, although some descendants worshiped idols.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره من أهل المعاني قوله: {وبني} دعاء لمن أذن الله في أن يدعو له

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Another view takes bani as his sons directly from his own loins.
rows.anchor: أو خص بهذه الدعوة أبناءه من صلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sanam is an image that is worshiped; its plural is asnam.
rows.anchor: والصنم: الصورة التي تعبد، وجمعه أصنام (¬4)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq and others say people went astray because of the idols; since idols cannot reason or act, the deed is attributed to them as to a house that captivates someone.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق وغيره: أي ضلوا بسببها؛ لأن الأصنام لا تعقل ولا تفعل شيئا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says following Ibrahim means following his religion of monotheism and knowledge of God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد على ديني بالتوحيد لك والمعرفة بك (¬1)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari explains he is of me as belonging to those who follow my religion and adhere to my covenant, as in the cited poem.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: يريد من المتدينين بميني المتمسكين بحبلي؛ كما قال (¬2):

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poem's speaker says he is not one of a person who attempts immorality among Asad, meaning he does not adhere to that person's covenant.
rows.anchor: إذا حاولت في أسد فجورا ... فإني لست منك ولست مني (¬3)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the disobedient person is forgiven if he repents and believes; Ibrahim is not saying God forgives someone who persists in unbelief.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: معناه ومن عصاني ثم تاب (¬5)، {فإنك غفور رحيم}] (¬6) له إن تاب وإن آمن

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil restricts the disobedience to matters below polytheism; Abu Bakr explains it as violating some religious laws while affirming monotheism, for which a Muslim may be forgiven if God wills.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ومن عصاني فيما دون الشرك فإنك غفور رحيم (¬7)، وشرح أبو بكر هذا

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr offers the possibility that the prayer preceded God's informing Ibrahim that shirk would not be forgiven; Ibrahim later disavowed his parents after learning they would not be forgiven.
rows.anchor: وشرح أبو بكر هذا فقال

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Another Abu Bakr explanation takes the disobedient person as persisting in unbelief; God is able to forgive by transferring him from unbelief to Islam and guiding him.
rows.anchor: وشرح أبو بكر هذا فقال

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra takes min as partitive: Ibrahim settled some of his descendants; Arabic can use min for a portion without stating the people affected, as in taking some food or water.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: ولم يأت منهم بشىء (¬1) يقع عليه الفعل، وهو حائز أن يقول: قد أصبنا من بني فلان

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr allows min to intensify the expression, with the sense I settled my descendants; he cites Dhu al-Rumma's use of min in poetry.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: ويجوز أن يقال: إن (من) دخلت لتوكيد الكلام، والتقدير: ربنا إني أسكنت ذريتي (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the descendants settled there as Ismail, one part of Ibrahim's progeny.
rows.anchor: قول ابن عباس في هذه الآية {إني أسكنت من ذريتي} يريد: إسماعيل (¬1)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the barren valley as the valley of Mecca; all of Mecca is a valley.
rows.anchor: {بواد غير ذي زرع} قال: يريد وادي مكة، ومكة كلها واد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali prefers the first analysis and glosses it as settling people from among Ibrahim's descendants, with the object people omitted because the verb settle makes it understood.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول: اختيار أبي علي، قال: معناه إني أسكنت من ذريتي ناسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that the Sacred House existed before being raised from the earth in the flood; Abraham settled Ismail in Mecca before they built it.
rows.anchor: قيل معناه: عند بيتك المحرم الذي كان قبل أن ترفعه من الأرض حتى رفعته أيام الطوفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the House was in God's prior knowledge as something that would arise in that valley.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عند بيتك المحرم الذي قد مضى في سابق علمك أنه يحدث في هذا الوادي (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses establishing prayer as worshiping God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ليعبدوك (¬4)

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد عن الأصمعي
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, transmitting from al-Asmaʿi, says hawa means falling from a height to a lower place.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيد عن الأصمعي قال: هوى يهوي هويا، إذا سقط من علو إلى سفل (¬5)

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrabi says an eagle hawat when it swoops down on prey or something else.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: هوت # العقاب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra glosses tahwi ilayhim as desiring or heading toward them, like someone going toward you; the word can mean descending or coming down.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء في هذه الآية: {تهوي إليهم} تريدهم؛ كما تقول: رأيت فلانا يهوي نحوك (¬4)

words: فَٱجْعَلْ أَفْـِٔدَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ تَهْوِىٓ إِلَيْهِمْ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, in Ata's transmission, says hearts yearn to visit God's House; the yearning concerns pilgrimage, not the descendants themselves, and the prayer benefits believers and Mecca's residents through pilgrims.
rows.anchor: فأما قول المفسرين؛ فقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: يريد تحن (¬7) إليهم زيارة بيتك (¬8)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains the hearts as being drawn toward them.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة في قوله: {تهوي إليهم}: تنزع إليهم (¬2)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq explains the prayer as asking that a group of people's hearts be drawn toward Ibrahim's descendants.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: أي: اجعل أفئدة جماعة من الناس تنزع إليهم (¬3)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says that if Ibrahim had asked for all people's hearts, Persia, Rome, the Turks, and India would crowd toward the place.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول مجاهد: لو قال: أفئدة الناس؛ لازدحمت عليه فارس والروم والترك والهند (¬4)

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says min limits the people to Muslims, since saying people's hearts without min would bring Jews, Christians, and Magians to pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: لو قال:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the people whose hearts are meant are believers, both his descendants and others.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في قوله: {أفئدة من الناس}: يريد من المؤمنين من ذريته ومن غير ذريته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi directs the reader to his explanation of this request in al-Baqara, at the parallel wording there.
rows.anchor: ذكرنا تفسيره في سورة البقرة عند قوله: {وارزق أهله من الثمرات} [البقرة: 126]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose is that they might affirm God's oneness and exalt Him.
rows.anchor: قال: يريد كي يوحدوك ويعظموك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrahim asks to be a constant establisher of prayer using an adjective, which is more enduring and emphatic than asking to perform the action; al-Wahidi links this discussion to another verse.
rows.anchor: ذكره على النعت ولم يذكره على الفعل؛ لأن النعت ألزم وأكثر من الفعل، كأنه قال: رب اجعلني

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads this as asking God to make some of Ibrahim's descendants people who establish prayer, like the partitive min in his earlier request and in 14:34.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أي: واجعل من ذريتي من يقيم الصلاة (¬4)، وهذا كما ذكرنا في قوله: {إني أسكنت من ذريتي}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says duʿa here means worship, as in the saying that supplication is the core of worship.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد عبادتي (¬5)

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says the cited poetic use of fuʾad for heart shows he sees no distinction between fuʾad and qalb.
rows.anchor: يعني أصاب قلبي، الأزهري: ولم أرهم يفرقون بينهما (¬4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading requires supplying a genitive: their hearts are possessors of emptiness, meaning they are empty.
rows.anchor: ويحتاج # في هذا التفسير إلى تقدير المضاف، كأن المعنى: وأفئدتهم ذات هواء؛ أي خالية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After completing the description of disbelievers and their resurrection state, the discourse returns to addressing the Prophet with a command to warn, linked to the preceding warning not to think God heedless.
rows.anchor: هذا عطف على قوله: {ولا تحسبن الله غافلا} لأنه قد تم وصف الكفار وحالهم عند البعث في القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the people to warn are Mecca's inhabitants; he adds that their following the Prophet would have left no pair in disagreement, and that Walid ibn al-Mughira's faith would have brought everyone along.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني أهل مكة (¬1)، قال: ولو أن أهل مكة اتبعوا النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - ما اختلف عليه اثنان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawma is the object of anẓir, as in warn him of punishment; it is not an adverb of time because the Prophet was not commanded to warn on that day.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {يوم يأتيهم العذاب} (يوم) مفعول به، والعامل فيه أنذرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause fa-yaqulu is coordinated with yaʾtihim and means that the wrongdoers will speak on that day.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {فيقول} عطف {يأتيهم}؛ يعني: فيقولون في ذلك اليوم، {الذين ظلموا}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses those who did wrong as those who associated partners with God.
rows.anchor: {الذين ظلموا} قال ابن عباس: يريد أشركوا (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: They ask for a short reprieve so they can answer God's call and follow the messengers; Ibn Abbas says they are asking to return to worldly life.
rows.anchor: {ربنا أخرنا إلى أجل قريب} استمهلوا مدة يسيرة لكي يجيبوا الدعوة ويتبعوا الرسل، قال ابن عباس: يريدون الرجعة إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-dhikr refers to the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {وقالوا يا أيها الذي نزل عليه الذكر} أي: القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, in Ata's transmission, says the address is mockery: if they believed the reminder had been sent down to him, they would not call him mad.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: هذا استهزاء منهم لو أيقنوا أنه نزل عليه الذكر

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali says the mockers do not believe revelation came to the Prophet; they mean one upon whom the reminder was sent in his own view or his followers' view, like taunts calling someone mighty or a magician.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو علي وجها آخر هو لأصحاب المعاني فقال: الذين يقولون للنبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - مجنون لا يقرون بإنزال الذكر عليه

rows.speaker: زهرة اليمن
rows.claim: The poet Zahra al-Yaman boasts that he is the splendid one and the flower of Yemen; the example shows an epithet can be spoken as the addressee's own claim.
rows.anchor: وقد قال زهرة اليمن (¬2): أبلغ كليبا وأبلغ عنك شاعرها ... أني الأغر وأني زهرة اليمن (¬3)

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarir answers Zahra al-Yaman, asking whether advice is already apparent in his identifying marks; this reinforces that the boastful epithet is in the speaker's own estimation.
rows.anchor: (وأجابه جرير: ألم يكن في وسوم قد وسمت بها ... من حان موعظة يازهرة اليمن) (¬4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Majnun derives from the root for covering: forms of the verb mean becoming or being made mad, and dense intertwined plants are called majnun because parts cover one another.
rows.anchor: يقال: جن فلان فهو مجنون، وقد أجنه الله، وبه جنون وجنة ومجنة، وأصله من الستر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the emphatic plural pronouns refer to God Himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد نفسه تبارك وتعالى.

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Language scholars say a king may use we for himself and his retinue, and this became a customary form even when the ruler acted alone.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة: هذا من كلام الملوك؛ الواحد منهم إذا فعل شيئا قال: نحن فعلنا

rows.speaker: عامة المفسرين
rows.claim: The generality of exegetes understand al-dhikr here as the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {نزلنا الذكر} يعني القرآن في قول عامة المفسرين (¬2)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God protects the revealed Qur'an from Satan adding falsehood or removing truth.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: أنزله الله وحفظه من أن يزيد الشيطان فيه باطلا أو يسقط منه حقا (¬3)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq likewise says the Qur'an is protected from addition and subtraction, as confirmed by the statement that falsehood cannot approach it.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال أبو إسحاق: أن يحفظ من أن يقع فيه زيادة أونقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions' collection of the Qur'an in written sheets was one means by which God preserved it; God provided them to do this when He willed its preservation.
rows.anchor: جمعهم للقرآن كان من أسباب حفظ الله إياه، ولما أراد حفظه قيضهم لذلك

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says the Companions collected the Qur'an to make it easier to access, memorize, and recite; it would not have been lost even without their work because God guaranteed its preservation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: إنهم أرادوا تسهيل القرآن على الناس وتقريب مطلبه

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi's associates take the verse as strong proof that the basmala is a Qur'anic verse in every surah: protection from addition and subtraction would otherwise fail, and suspecting the Companions of adding it would also permit suspecting omission.
rows.anchor: قال أصحابنا: هذه الآية دلالة قوية على كون التسمية آية من كل سورة (¬1)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra allows the pronoun in lahu to refer to Muhammad, yielding the meaning We are protectors of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وحكى الفراء جواز رجوع الكناية في (له) إلى محمد -صلى الله عليه وسلم- المعنى: وإنا لمحمد حافظون (¬2)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari prefers the pronoun's first referent, the Qur'an: mentioning the sending and the sent thing makes its recipient understood, as in the Qur'an's unexpressed pronoun at 97:1.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: ولما ذكر الإنزال والمنزل دل ذلك على المنزل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi calls the first interpretation clearer and more consistent with the surface sense of the revelation.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول هو أوضح القولين، وأحسنها مشابهة لظاهر التنزيل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi glosses forming Adam as shaping and proportioning his figure into a human form.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى {فإذا سويته} قال الكلبي: يقول جصعت خلقه يعني عدلت صورته وسويته بالصورة الإنسانية (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafkh means causing air to flow into something.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ونفخت فيه من روحي} النفخ إجراء الريح في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spirit is a subtle body by which the body lives; al-Wahidi defers fuller discussion to the verse asking about the spirit.
rows.anchor: والروح جسم رقيق يحيا به البدن، ونذكر الكلام فيها عند قوله: {ويسألونك عن الروح} [الإسراء: 85]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God attributes Adam's spirit to Himself as an honor and distinction, in the sense of a possession attribution.
rows.anchor: وأضاف روح آدم إليه تكرمة لما كرمه وشرفه، وهي إضافة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-qaʿu is an imperative derived from falling.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {فقعوا له} أمر من الوقوع

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and the exegetes say the angels prostrated to Adam as a greeting of respect, not as an act of worship; al-Wahidi refers to discussions of its manner and greeting-prostration elsewhere.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: فخروا له ساجدين سجدة تحية ولم تكن سجدة طاعة، ونحو هذا قال جميع المفسرين (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the creator is God and those who do not create are the idols mentioned in this surah, as in the statement this is God's creation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ما ذكر في هذه السورة، ومن يخلق هو الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains the use of man for idols by their association in the sentence with the Creator; Arabs similarly pair a human rider with his camel under man.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: والعرب تقول: اشتبه علي الراكب وجمله، فلا أدري من ذا ومن ذا؟ حيث جمعها وأحدهما إنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the idols are addressed as man because people worshiped them, just as a verse asks whether idols have feet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم لما عبدوها ذكرت بلفظ (من) (¬4)؛ كقوله: {ألهم أرجل} الآية [الأعراف: 195]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the question addresses the polytheists: will they not take heed as the believers did?
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد المشركين، يقول: أفلا تتعظون كما اتعظ المؤمنون (¬1)

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi's associates argue that the verse establishes one Creator, distinguished from creatures by the power to originate creation; one who claims to create his own acts makes himself God's partner in creation.
rows.anchor: قال أصحابنا: وهذه الآية دليل على أن الخالق واحد، وإنما يتميز الخالق من المخلوق بالقدرة على اختراع الخلق

rows.speaker: أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Exegetes say the verse denies that creator and noncreator can be treated equally in worship, just as one should not give equal thanks to a benefactor and a non-benefactor.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل التأويل: معنى هذه الآية: إنكار تشبيه من يخلق بمن لا يخلق بالتسوية بينهما في العبادة

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: The general reading has the second-person form taʾ, matching the preceding address to disbelievers; Asim reads yaʾ, reporting about the polytheists who worship idols, then describing those idols.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {والذين يدعون} قراءة العامة بالتاء (¬6)؛ لأن ما قبل هذه الآية كلها خطاب للكفار، وقرأ عاصم بالياء في: {يدعون} (¬7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people possess runs out and means the transient world; what is with God is lasting reward and honor.
rows.anchor: {ما عندكم ينفد}، أي: يفنى وينقطع، يعني الدنيا، {وما عند الله}، أي: من الثواب والكرامة، {باق}: دائم لا ينقطع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the reward never runs out: whatever is taken or eaten is replaced; this refutes those who say Paradise's pleasures will end.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد لا ينفد؛ كلما أخذت منه وأكلت منه صار مكانه مثله، فمعنى [لا] (¬3) يفنى هذا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the patient are those steadfast in their religion and in avoiding what God forbade.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد على دينهم وعما نهاهم الله (¬4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best deeds mean acts of obedience: permissible good actions deserve no reward, while obedience is the best and earns the promised reward; rewarding by the best deeds entails forgiveness of sins.
rows.anchor: {بأحسن ما كانوا يعملون} يعني الطاعات، وجعلها أحسن أعمالهم؛ لأن ما عداها من الحسن مباح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns against false oaths and urges people to fulfill covenants and oaths.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآيات زجر عن الأيمان الكاذبة فيما كانت، وحث على الوفاء بالعهود والأيمان

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says these verses were revealed about Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAbis al-Kindi and his opponent ʿAydan ibn Ashwaʿ over a parcel of land; as Imruʾ al-Qays prepared to swear, he wept and admitted the other's right.
rows.anchor: وذكر الكلبي: أن هذه الآيات نزلت في امرئ القيس بن عابس الكندي (¬2)، وفي خصمه عيدان ابن أشوع (¬3)
